name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
description: One of the oldest known members of the human lineage, known mainly from a cranium ('Toumaï') found in the Djurab Desert of Chad. Its age is around 7 million years, near the time hominins and chimpanzees diverged, and whether it walked upright is debated.

media.title: Toumaï, the New Ancestor

name: Orrorin tugenensis
description: Early hominin from the Tugen Hills of Kenya, about 6 million years old. Thigh-bone fossils have been argued to show upright walking, though this is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The First Humans After The Human-Chimp Split: Orrorin Tugenensis

name: Ardipithecus kadabba
description: Late Miocene hominin from the Middle Awash of Ethiopia, known from fragmentary remains. Often seen as an ancestor of Ardipithecus ramidus.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Ardipithecus (That We Know Of) | The Evolution of Us

name: Ardipithecus ramidus
description: Early hominin from Aramis, Ethiopia, about 4.4 million years old, known from the partial skeleton 'Ardi'. It combined tree-climbing adaptations with a pelvis suited to upright walking.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Discovering Ardi - How Ardi Walked

name: Australopithecus anamensis
description: Early australopith from the Turkana basin of Kenya and Ethiopia, around 4.2 to 3.8 million years ago, often regarded as ancestral to A. afarensis. One of the earliest clearly bipedal hominins.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Lucy's Grandad? Examining Australopithecus Anamensis

name: Australopithecus afarensis
description: Small-brained, habitually bipedal hominin of East Africa, known from the 'Lucy' skeleton (Hadar, Ethiopia) and the Laetoli footprints (Tanzania).
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Life And Death 3,000,000 Years Ago

name: Kenyanthropus platyops
description: Hominin known from a flat-faced skull found near Lake Turkana in Kenya, about 3.5 million years old. Whether it is a distinct genus or a variant of another australopith is disputed.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Kenyanthropus platyops: The Flat Faced Hominin Who Lived Alongside Lucy

name: Australopithecus africanus
description: Gracile australopith of South Africa, first recognised from the Taung Child in 1924. Found at cave sites such as Sterkfontein and Makapansgat; dating of these deposits is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The Missing Link That Wasn't

name: Paranthropus aethiopicus
description: Early robust australopith known from the 'Black Skull' of West Turkana, Kenya, and remains in the Omo Valley. Probably ancestral to later robust forms.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Paranthropus aethiopicus: The Black Skull

description: Australopith from Bouri in Ethiopia's Middle Awash, about 2.5 million years old. Found near animal bones with cut marks, which fed debate on early stone-tool use.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Australopithecus garhi | Human Evolution

name: Homo habilis
description: Early member of the genus Homo from East Africa, long associated with the first stone tools. Its status as a distinct species is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Homo Habilis – The Handy Man | Human Evolution Documentary

name: Paranthropus robustus
description: Robust australopith of South Africa, found in the Cradle of Humankind caves including Swartkrans, Kromdraai and Drimolen. Lived alongside early Homo.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Paranthropus Evolution

name: Homo erectus
description: Long-legged, larger-brained hominin and the first to spread widely beyond Africa, reaching the Caucasus (Dmanisi), China (Zhoukoudian) and Java (Sangiran, Ngandong).
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The Humans That Lived Before Us

name: Homo rudolfensis
description: Early Homo known mainly from the skull KNM-ER 1470 at Koobi Fora, Kenya. Whether it is a separate species from Homo habilis is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Homo Rudolfensis: Humanity’s Forgotten Ancestor

name: Australopithecus sediba
description: Hominin from Malapa cave in South Africa, close to 2 million years old, with a mix of australopith and Homo-like features. Known from well-preserved partial skeletons.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Lee Berger: Rewriting human history

name: Paranthropus boisei
description: Robust East African hominin with massive jaws and chewing teeth, nicknamed 'Nutcracker Man'. Found at Olduvai Gorge, Koobi Fora and other sites; its diet was probably mostly tough plant matter.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The Diet Paradox: What Did Nutcracker Man Actually Eat?

name: Homo antecessor
description: Hominin known from Gran Dolina at Atapuerca, Spain, about 800,000 years old. Remains show some of the earliest evidence of humans in western Europe and its placement in the family tree is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: New Homo Antecessor Discoveries at Atapuerca

name: Homo heidelbergensis
description: Middle Pleistocene hominin known from sites in Europe and Africa, often seen as close to the ancestry of Neanderthals and modern humans. Which fossils belong to the species is debated.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The Story of Homo Heidelbergensis | Ancient Human Documentary

name: Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal)
description: Cold-adapted hominins of Europe and western Asia who made sophisticated stone tools and buried their dead. They interbred with modern humans and disappeared about 40,000 years ago. The oldest site here, Sima de los Huesos, is usually treated as an early member of the Neanderthal line.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Homo Neanderthalensis: 'The Neanderthal Man'

name: Homo sapiens
description: Anatomically modern humans, first appearing in Africa at least 300,000 years ago and spreading across the world. Site points shown here end around 10,000 BCE.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: A Crash Course In Human Evolution With Anthropologist Chris Stringer

name: Homo naledi
description: Small-brained hominin from the Rising Star cave system in South Africa, dated to roughly 335,000 to 236,000 years ago, so it lived alongside early modern humans.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: The Extinct Human Species Found In Remote Cave Chambers

name: Denisovans
description: Archaic human group known mainly from DNA and a few fossils from Denisova Cave in Siberia and Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau. They interbred with both Neanderthals and modern humans.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Where are all the Denisovans? Ancient DNA

name: Homo luzonensis
description: Hominin known from teeth and bones from Callao Cave on Luzon, Philippines, at least 67,000 years old. Its relationships to other hominins are unclear.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Homo luzonensis: Another 'hobbit' species

name: Homo floresiensis
description: Small-bodied hominin from Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia, nicknamed the 'Hobbit'. Skeletal remains are dated to roughly 100,000 to 60,000 years ago.
image_credit: AI-generated illustration, not a scientific reconstruction

media.title: Homo Floresiensis - Ancient Human

name: Lomekwian
description: The oldest known stone tool industry, from Lomekwi 3 in West Turkana, Kenya, about 3.3 million years ago. It predates the genus Homo, and its makers are unknown.

media.title: The oldest archaeological site in the world

name: Oldowan
description: Earliest widespread stone tool industry, made of simple flakes and choppers struck from cobbles. Found from about 2.6 million years ago across Africa and into western Asia.

media.title: The Oldowan stone tool

name: Acheulean
description: Stone tool tradition best known for large, shaped hand axes, associated mainly with Homo erectus and later hominins. It lasted well over a million years across Africa, Europe and South Asia.

media.title: Acheulean technology and how to make a handaxe

name: Middle Stone Age (Africa)
description: African counterpart of the Middle Palaeolithic, beginning about 300,000 years ago. Sites such as Blombos Cave have early evidence of ochre use, engraving and bead-making.

media.title: Inside Africa's hidden history of early humans

fallback_image.label: Middle Stone Age and Neanderthal toolmakers in general

name: Levallois / Mousterian
description: Middle Palaeolithic tool tradition built on prepared-core (Levallois) flake technology, linked mainly with Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia and also with early modern humans in the Levant.

media.title: Levallois core technology: an alternative way of making stone tools

fallback_image.label: Middle Stone Age and Neanderthal toolmakers in general

name: Aurignacian
description: Early Upper Palaeolithic culture of Europe linked with modern humans, with blade tools, bone points, ornaments, early figurative art and musical instruments.

media.title: How the Aurignacians conquered Ice Age Europe

name: Gravettian
description: Upper Palaeolithic culture across Europe, known for small 'Venus' figurines, mammoth-bone dwellings and pointed blades.

media.title: The Gravettian Culture: Ice Age mammoth hunters

name: Solutrean
description: Upper Palaeolithic culture of France and Iberia, noted for finely pressure-flaked leaf-shaped points.

media.title: The Solutrean Culture

name: Magdalenian
description: Late Upper Palaeolithic culture of western Europe known for cave art, such as Altamira, and for carved bone and antler tools.

media.title: The Magdalenian Culture

name: Natufian
description: Late Epipalaeolithic culture of the Levant, with some of the earliest semi-permanent villages and intensive wild-cereal harvesting just before farming began.

media.title: Who were the Natufian people?

name: Clovis
description: Widespread North American stone tool tradition around 13,000 years ago, characterised by fluted spear points.

media.title: The Clovis Culture

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic
description: Early farming societies of the Levant and southeast Anatolia before pottery, including the monumental site Göbekli Tepe and the walled settlement at Jericho.

media.title: Stone Age temple mystery (Göbekli Tepe)

name: Starčevo–Körös–Criș culture
description: First farming culture of the inland Balkans and the Carpathian Basin, c. 6200–4500 BCE, known as Starčevo in Serbia, Körös in Hungary and Criș in Romania. It carried farming and pottery north from the Aegean and preceded the Linear Pottery culture.

media.title: Unearthing the Starčevo Culture: Europe's early Neolithic farmers

name: Cardial culture
description: Early Neolithic culture of the western Mediterranean, named after pottery decorated by pressing cockle shells (Cardium) into the clay. Cardial communities spread farming rapidly along the coasts from Italy to Portugal.

media.title: What was the Cardial culture of southern Europe?

name: Linear Pottery (LBK)
description: First farming culture of central Europe, with long timber houses and pottery decorated with linear incised patterns.

media.title: The enormous longhouses of the Linear Pottery Culture

name: Ertebølle culture
description: Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherer and fisher culture of southern Scandinavia and northern Germany, c. 5400–3950 BCE, which made pottery and left large shell middens. Also called Ertebølle–Ellerbek.

media.title: Tranchet axeheads in prehistoric Europe

name: Vinča culture
description: Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, c. 5400–4500 BCE, named after the tell of Vinča-Belo Brdo near Belgrade. Known for large settlements, dark burnished pottery, figurines and early copper working.

media.title: Europe's first civilization: the Vinča Culture

name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
description: Neolithic–Chalcolithic culture of Romania, Moldova and Ukraine, c. 5050–2950 BCE, famous for painted pottery and giant settlements of thousands of houses between the Carpathians and the Dnieper.

media.title: Cucuteni-Trypillia Culture: ancient European civilization

name: Lengyel culture
description: Neolithic culture of the Middle Danube, c. 5000–4000 BCE, centred on Hungary, Slovakia, Austria and Moravia, known for painted pottery and circular ditched enclosures (rondels). Named after Lengyel in Tolna county, Hungary.

media.title: Svodín: a Neolithic settlement of the Lengyel culture

name: Chasséen culture
description: Middle Neolithic culture of France, c. 4500–3500 BCE, spread from the south across much of the country. Named after the site at Chassey-le-Camp in Saône-et-Loire.

media.title: Chassey-le-Camp : visite sur le site archéologique

name: Badarian culture
description: Early farming culture of Upper Egypt, named after the El-Badari region, which flourished between about 4400 and 4000 BCE and preceded the Naqada culture.

media.title: Predynastic Egypt: before the pharaohs and pyramids

name: Michelsberg culture
description: Neolithic culture of west-central Europe along both sides of the Rhine, c. 4400–3500 BCE, known for causewayed enclosures. Named after the Michaelsberg hill near Untergrombach in Baden-Württemberg.

media.title: Die Michelsberger Kultur, ein kleiner Einblick

name: Funnelbeaker culture
description: Neolithic farming culture of north-central Europe and southern Scandinavia (TRB), named after its funnel-necked beakers. It was succeeded in the north by the Single Grave culture around 2800 BCE.

media.title: The Funnelbeaker Culture: Neolithic farmers of northern Europe

name: Naqada culture
description: Chalcolithic culture of Predynastic Egypt, named after the town of Naqada, c. 4000–3000 BCE. Through its phases Naqada I–III it led into the first Egyptian dynasties.

media.title: Cultures of Predynastic Egypt (Badarian & Naqada)

name: Baden culture
description: Copper Age culture of central and southeastern Europe, c. 3520–2690 BCE, found from Moravia and southern Poland to Hungary, Slovakia, eastern Austria and northern Croatia. Also called Baden–Pécel.

media.title: Which ancient society really invented the wheel?

fallback_image.label: Copper and Bronze Age Europe in general

name: Globular Amphora culture
description: Late Neolithic culture of central and eastern Europe, c. 3400–2800 BCE, named after its round-bellied pots with two to four handles. It preceded the Corded Ware culture in much of its area.

media.title: The Fall of Neolithic Europe: the Globular Amphora Culture

fallback_image.label: Copper and Bronze Age Europe in general

name: Corded Ware culture
description: Broad Late Neolithic to early Bronze Age horizon across northern and central Europe, named after pottery decorated with cord impressions and known for single burials under mounds. Includes the Single Grave culture of southern Scandinavia, northern Germany and the Low Countries.

media.title: The Corded Ware Culture (3000 BC - 2300 BC)

fallback_image.label: Copper and Bronze Age Europe in general

name: Bell Beaker culture
description: Archaeological culture of western and central Europe at the start of the Bronze Age, named after its inverted-bell drinking vessels. It varied strongly by region and lasted until between about 2300 and 1650 BCE depending on the area.

media.title: Meet the Bell Beakers: the culture that changed Europe

fallback_image.label: Copper and Bronze Age Europe in general

name: Únětice culture
description: Early Bronze Age culture of central Europe, c. 2300–1600 BCE, centred on Bohemia, Moravia, central Germany and western Poland. Named after the village of Únětice near Prague; the Nebra sky disc belongs to its world.

media.title: Kings of Bronze Age Europe: the Únětice Culture

fallback_image.label: Copper and Bronze Age Europe in general

description: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates, home to the earliest cities and a succession of Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian states.
name: Mesopotamia

media.title: 8. The Sumerians - Fall of the First Cities

name: Sumerian City-States
description: A network of pioneering Bronze Age city-states—including Uruk, Ur, and Eridu—in the river valleys of southern Mesopotamia. Sumerians developed the world's earliest known writing system (cuneiform), monumental mudbrick ziggurats, advanced irrigation networks, and complex municipal law codes.

media.title: Ancient Mesopotamia: The First Cities in History | Sumer and the Urban Revolution

name: Elam
description: An ancient civilization centered in southwestern Iran across Khuzestan and the Zagros highlands, with principal capitals at Susa and Anshan. Contemporaries and frequent rivals of Sumer, Babylon, and Assyria, the Elamites developed their own Linear Elamite and cuneiform scripts, monumental brick ziggurats like Chogha Zanbil, and deeply influenced the rise of the Persian Empire.

media.title: The Ancient Kingdom of Elam, what was it?

description: Pharaonic civilisation along the Nile, from the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and the intermediate periods between them, with foreign rule by Hyksos and Assyrians in places.
name: Ancient Egypt

media.title: 18. Egypt - Fall of the Pharaohs

name: Early Dynastic Period of Egypt
description: The formative era of unified Egyptian civilization (First and Second Dynasties) following the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under Narmer. Governing from the royal seat of Thinis and Memphis, this period consolidated divine kingship, codified hieroglyphic writing, established mortuary complexes at Abydos, and laid the foundations of pharaonic statecraft.

media.title: The Early Dynastic Period: A Complete Overview (3150 BC–2686 BC)

name: Indus Valley Civilization
description: A major Bronze Age urban civilization spanning modern Pakistan and northwestern India, centered along the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra river basins. Renowned for sophisticated urban grid planning, baked-brick architecture, advanced hydraulic sanitation systems, and standardized weights at metropolises like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, the civilization maintained extensive maritime trade with ancient Mesopotamia.

media.title: The Rise and Fall of the Indus Valley Civilization

name: Old Kingdom of Egypt
description: Celebrated as the 'Age of the Pyramids', the Old Kingdom (Third to Sixth Dynasties) was an era of dynamic internal security, centralized pharaonic power, and monumental building along the Nile. Governed from Memphis, pharaohs marshaled royal labor to erect the Great Pyramids and the Sphinx at Giza, institutionalizing enduring religious and funerary traditions.

media.title: The Old Kingdom: A Complete Overview (2686 BC–2181 BC)

name: Akkadian Empire
description: Regarded as the world's first multi-national empire, founded by Sargon the Great around 2334 BCE in central Mesopotamia. Uniting Akkadian and Sumerian speakers under centralized rule, the empire fostered major artistic, administrative, and military innovations across the Fertile Crescent before collapsing amid climatic disruption and regional unrest.

media.title: SARGON OF AKKAD - The Man Who Built the First Empire

name: Lower Egypt
description: The northern delta region of ancient Egypt where the Nile fans out into the Mediterranean Sea, characterized by lush papyrus marshes, maritime trade, and fertile agriculture. Historically symbolized by the red crown (Deshret) and the cobra goddess Wadjet, Lower Egypt united with Upper Egypt to form the dual pharaonic monarchy.

media.title: The Surprising Story of Egypt's Two Kingdoms!

name: Upper Egypt
description: The southern riverine expanse of ancient Egypt stretching along the narrow Nile Valley from the First Cataract at Aswan to Memphis. Represented by the white crown (Hedjet) and the vulture goddess Nekhbet, Upper Egypt was the heartland of early state formation, renowned for spiritual centers at Abydos, Thebes, and Hierakonpolis.

media.title: Egypt's Secret Unification: The Story They Don't Teach

name: Gutian Dynasty
description: A line of rulers originating from the Zagros Mountains who seized control of central and southern Mesopotamia following the decline of the Akkadian Empire. Though remembered in later Sumerian king lists as destructive overlords, Gutian kings ruled for roughly a century before being ousted by Utu-hengal of Uruk.

media.title: Were Gutians Tocharians?

name: Middle Kingdom of Egypt
description: The golden age of classical Egyptian civilization (Eleventh to Thirteenth Dynasties), reunified by Mentuhotep II following the First Intermediate Period. Ruled from Thebes and Itjtawy, this era is revered for classical Egyptian literature, monumental irrigation projects in the Faiyum oasis, fortress architecture in Nubia, and an expressive, reflective royal art style.

media.title: Ancient Egypt Part 2: The Middle Kingdom (2000 – 1500 BCE)

name: Assyria
description: A major ancient Mesopotamian civilization centered along the upper Tigris River in modern northern Iraq. Spanning Old, Middle, and Imperial periods, Assyria developed into a formidable military and commercial power renowned for sophisticated statecraft, monumental palaces, and the preservation of vast cuneiform libraries.

media.title: The Epic of Ancient Assyria - PART I: Early Ashur and the Old Assyrian Kingdom (c. 3000-1400 BC)

name: Babylonia
description: An influential cultural and political state in central-southern Mesopotamia, centered on the ancient metropolis of Babylon along the Euphrates. Under Hammurabi and later dynasties, Babylonia became famed across the ancient world for its monumental architecture, astronomical scholarship, mathematical innovations, and enduring legal traditions.

media.title: Rise of Babylon and Hammurabi - Ancient Mesopotamia DOCUMENTARY

name: Hyksos
description: Rulers of Levantine origin who established Egypt's Fifteenth Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period, ruling from their fortified capital of Avaris in the eastern Nile Delta. Their presence introduced horse-drawn chariots, composite bows, and improved bronze metallurgy into Egypt before their expulsion by native Theban pharaohs.

media.title: Ancient Egypt Dynasty by Dynasty - Dynasties XV & XVI - The Arrival of the Hyksos

name: First Sealand Dynasty
description: An enigmatic dynasty of kings based in the marshlands and coastal plains of southern Mesopotamia, ruling independently of Babylonian control during the second millennium BCE. Preserving ancient Sumerian cultural traditions, the Sealand monarchs successfully resisted Kassite expansion until their territory was eventually incorporated into the Kassite Babylonian state.

media.title: The First Dynasty of the Sealand and the Last Days of the Old Babylonian Kingdom (c. 1730-1460 BC)

description: The early dynasties and states of China: Shang and Zhou, the many states of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, then the Qin and Han unifications.
name: Ancient China

media.title: 10. The Han Dynasty - The First Empire in Flames

name: Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt
description: The ruling house of the Hyksos during the Second Intermediate Period, established by Levantine leaders who governed northern Egypt from their fortified delta capital of Avaris. Introducing bronze weaponry, composite bows, and horse-drawn chariots into the Nile Valley, the dynasty maintained commercial networks until driven out by native Theban pharaohs.

media.title: Hyksos: The Mysterious ,,Foreign Kings'' of Egypt

name: Hittites
description: A major Bronze Age empire established by Indo-European speakers in central Anatolia, centered at their fortified capital of Hattusa. Pioneers in early iron metallurgy and chariot warfare, the Hittites expanded across modern Turkey and northern Syria, signing the world's earliest known parity peace treaty with Ramesses II of Egypt.

media.title: The Entire History Of The Hittites / Ancient History Documentary

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Minoan civilization
description: An advanced Bronze Age maritime civilization that flourished on the Mediterranean island of Crete, centered at the labyrinthine palace complex of Knossos. Famed for vibrant frescoes, unfortified settlements, seafaring commerce, and the undeciphered Linear A script, Minoan society exerted immense cultural influence across the Aegean before its Bronze Age decline.

media.title: The Truth About Minoan Weapons and Warfare

name: Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt
description: The native Theban dynasty of Upper Egypt during the late Second Intermediate Period that mounted a national war of liberation against the northern Hyksos occupiers. Under martial rulers like Seqenenre Tao, Kamose, and Ahmose I, Theban armies pushed northward, capturing Avaris and ushering in the glorious New Kingdom.

media.title: Seqenenre Tao (1558-1554 BC)

name: Shang Dynasty
description: The earliest historically confirmed Chinese dynasty, ruling the fertile Yellow River valley from capitals like Anyang (Yinxu) between c. 1600 and 1046 BCE. Renowned for masterful piece-mold ritual bronze casting, horse-drawn chariot warfare, and the earliest surviving Chinese writing inscribed on divination oracle bones.

media.title: [Documentary] China's Bronze Age - Shang Dynasty (1760 - 1520 BC)

name: Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt
description: A regional Theban dynasty of Upper Egypt that governed the Nile Valley between Thebes and Elephantine during the turbulent Second Intermediate Period. Besieged by devastating local famines, northern pressure from the Hyksos, and southern attacks from Kush, this resilient kingdom maintained native pharaonic traditions until succeeded by the Seventeenth Dynasty.

media.title: The Second Intermediate Period: A Complete Overview (1700–1550 BC)

description: The Bronze Age Mycenaeans, the Dark Age that followed, and the city-states and leagues of the Archaic and Classical Greek world.
name: Ancient Greece

media.title: The Entire History of Ancient Greece (1100–146 BC)

name: Mitanni
description: A powerful Hurrian-speaking kingdom centered in northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia that flourished as a major Near Eastern empire during the mid-second millennium BCE. Renowned for horse breeding and chariot warfare, Mitanni rivaled Egypt and the Hittite Empire before falling to Assyrian and Hittite expansion.

media.title: History of the Hurrian Kingdom of the Mitanni

name: Mycenaean Greece
description: The mainland Greek civilization of the Late Bronze Age, immortalized in Homeric epic poetry, centered at fortified citadels such as Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos. Governed by warrior-kings (wanakes), the Mycenaeans developed the Linear B syllabic script—the earliest attested Greek—and established trade networks across the Mediterranean before collapsing around 1200 BCE.

media.title: The Bronze Age Civilization That Became Greek Mythology — The Mycenaeans

name: New Kingdom of Egypt
description: The imperial zenith of pharaonic Egypt (Eighteenth to Twentieth Dynasties), forged by warrior pharaohs like Thutmose III, Hatshepsut, and Ramesses II. Stretching from Nubia to the Euphrates, the empire amassed unprecedented wealth, constructing monumental temple complexes at Karnak and Luxor and magnificent royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

media.title: New Kingdom Egypt: A Complete Overview From Ahmose to Ramesses

name: Neo-Hittite states
description: A collection of Luwian- and Aramean-speaking Iron Age successor principalities across southeastern Anatolia and northern Syria following the collapse of the Hittite Empire. These small kingdoms—such as Carchemish and Tabal—preserved distinctive Hittite artistic, architectural, and hieroglyphic traditions until swallowed by the expanding Neo-Assyrian Empire.

media.title: The Hittites (Part 22): The Rise and Fall of the Neo Hittite Kingdoms (c.1207-700 BC)

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Philistia
description: A confederation of five coastal city-states—Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath—established in southwestern Canaan during the Early Iron Age. Associated with the migrating Sea Peoples, the Philistines introduced distinctive Aegean-style pottery and advanced ironworking techniques, frequently clashing with neighboring Israelites and Canaanites.

media.title: Who were the Philistines? (History of the Philistines explained)

fallback_image.label: Phoenician and Carthaginian world in general

name: Phoenicia
description: Ancient Semitic seafaring civilization originating in the coastal Levant (modern Lebanon and coastal Syria). Renowned as master mariners, traders, and artisans, the Phoenicians established trade networks and colonies across the Mediterranean—most notably Carthage—and developed the phonetic alphabet that became the ancestor of Greek, Latin, and modern writing systems.

media.title: A Brief History of the Phoenicians (1500 - 300 BC)

fallback_image.label: Phoenician and Carthaginian world in general

name: Greek Dark Ages
description: The transitional period of ancient Greek history following the catastrophic Late Bronze Age collapse of Mycenaean palace culture. Characterized initially by depopulation, the loss of Linear B literacy, and regional isolation, this era witnessed the adoption of ironworking, the spread of the Greek alphabet, and the foundational emergence of the independent polis (city-state).

media.title: Did You Know Ancient Greece Had Its Dark Ages?

name: Kingdom of Israel
description: An Iron Age kingdom in the northern central highlands and fertile Jezreel Valley of the southern Levant, with Samaria as its prominent capital. Boasting significant agricultural wealth and international trade links, the kingdom was a major regional power before its destruction and population deportation by the Neo-Assyrian Empire in 720 BCE.

media.title: Kings of Israel & Judah Family Tree

fallback_image.label: Ancient Levant and Arabia in general

name: Kingdom of Kush
description: A powerful ancient Nubian civilization centered along the Middle Nile in modern Sudan, with historic capitals at Kerma, Napata, and Meroë. Famed for archery, gold mining, and distinctive steep-sided pyramids, the Kushites conquered Egypt in the 8th century BCE to rule as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty before later flourishing as an ironworking empire.

media.title: Kingdom of Kush - History Of Africa with Zeinab Badawi

name: Zhou Dynasty
description: The longest-lasting dynasty in Chinese history (1046–256 BCE), which overthrew the Shang and established the political doctrine of the 'Mandate of Heaven'. Initially ruling through a decentralized feudal network of kinship fiefs (fengjian), the Western Zhou fostered classical Chinese cultural, ritual, and philosophical foundations.

media.title: [Documentary] Origin of Li and Yue - Zhou Dynasty (1046 -256 BC)

name: Kingdom of Judah
description: An Iron Age kingdom centered in the southern Judean hill country of the Levant, governed from Jerusalem by the Davidic dynasty. Emerging after the division of the united monarchy, Judah maintained religious and cultural identity under Assyrian and Babylonian vassalage until Jerusalem was sacked by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 BCE.

media.title: History of Ancient Israel and Judah explained in 5 minutes

The alliance secured Aegean sea routes and curbed Spartan ambitions, but dissolved following the Social War when key allies rebelled against renewed Athenian dominance.

name: Zhongshan
description: A unique kingdom in the central plains of modern Hebei, founded by the semi-nomadic White Di (Baidi) pastoralists during the Warring States period. Remarkably synthesizing Steppe nomadic traditions with sophisticated Zhou ritual culture and bronze casting, Zhongshan built fortified capitals and resisted Zhao and Wei invasions for over a century before falling in 296 BCE.

media.title: The King Who Dressed Like a Nomad | Zhao Conquers Zhongshan (307–296 BCE)

name: Qataban
description: An ancient South Arabian kingdom centered in the Baihan valley of western Yemen, with its capital at the merchant hub of Timna. Governed by sophisticated agricultural water codes and legal decrees, Qataban prospered by taxing trade along the incense route until eclipsed by neighboring Saba and Himyar.

name: Thebans
description: The ancient Greek citizens and military power of Thebes, the preeminent city of the Boeotian confederacy in central Greece. Reaching its geopolitical zenith under Epaminondas in the 4th century BCE, Thebes broke Spartan hegemony and liberated the Messenian helots before being destroyed by Alexander the Great following an uprising in 335 BCE.

media.title: When 6,000 Thebans CRUSHED 10,000 Spartans | Battle of Leuctra

name: Kingdom of Bithynia
description: A Hellenistic kingdom located in northwestern Anatolia bordering the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea, centered on cities like Nicomedia. Governed by a resilient local Thracian dynasty, Bithynia maintained autonomy against neighboring Diadochi kingdoms before its last king, Nicomedes IV, bequeathed the realm to the Roman Republic in 74 BCE.

media.title: Roman Bithynia and Pontus

name: Minyue
description: An ancient Baiyue kingdom located in the mountainous coastal river valleys of modern Fujian province in southeastern China. Flourishing from the 4th to late 2nd century BCE, Minyue maintained fortified towns, specialized metallurgy, and maritime trade before being annexed by Emperor Wu of Han.

media.title: Minyue Ancient Fujian

name: Nanda Empire
description: The powerful pan-Gangetic empire established in the 4th century BCE by Mahapadma Nanda, who overthrew the Shaishunagas and conquered numerous northern Indian kingdoms. Governed from Pataliputra, the Nandas accumulated immense treasury wealth and commanded a vast standing army of 200,000 infantry and 3,000 war elephants that discouraged Alexander the Great from advancing into India.

media.title: The Empire So Wealthy and So Hated That Alexander's Own Army Refused to Fight It

name: Cyrenaica
description: A prosperous Greek settlement region on the Mediterranean coast of eastern Libya, founded in the 7th century BCE around the city of Cyrene. Renowned for its philosophers, horse racing, and monopoly on the prized medicinal plant silphium, Cyrenaica evolved from an independent monarchy into a Hellenistic kingdom before Roman annexation.

media.title: The True Story of Ancient Greece's Lost City in Africa

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
description: The wealthy Hellenistic kingdom founded in Egypt by Ptolemy I Soter, Alexander the Great's companion general, which ruled from 305 to 30 BCE. Governed from Alexandria—a global capital of scholarship and commerce boasting the Great Library and Pharos lighthouse—the dynasty blended Greek and Egyptian traditions, concluding with Cleopatra VII's defeat by Octavian.

media.title: Ptolemy I Soter - First Pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt Documentary

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: A major kingdom in the Armenian Highlands that reached imperial status under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE, stretching from the Caspian to the Mediterranean. Buffering the Roman and Parthian empires, Armenia fostered a distinct national identity and became the world's first state to officially adopt Christianity in 301 CE.

name: Athenian Coalition
description: The alliance of Aegean and Ionian maritime city-states led by democratic Athens—originating from the Delian League—during the protracted Peloponnesian War against Sparta (431–404 BCE). Powered by Athenian naval supremacy (triremes) and funded by tributary wealth, the coalition defended maritime commerce across the Aegean until its catastrophic defeat at Aegospotami.

media.title: The Rise of Athens: The Delian League (479-445 BC)

name: Kingdom of Lysimachus
description: The Hellenistic realm carved out by Lysimachus, a companion general of Alexander the Great who ruled Thrace, northwestern Anatolia, and Macedonia following the Battle of Ipsus. Built around strategic strongholds like Lysimachia, his short-lived kingdom collapsed when Lysimachus was defeated and killed by Seleucus I at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BCE.

media.title: The Forgotten King: Lysimachus and the Rise of the Diadochi

name: Laomedon
description: The satrapy of Syria and Phoenicia assigned to Alexander the Great's general Laomedon of Mytilene following the Partition of Babylon in 323 BCE. Controlling vital Levantine ports and timber reserves, Laomedon ruled briefly before being ousted and captured by Ptolemy I Soter's forces during the Wars of the Diadochi.

name: Perdiccas
description: The central regency of the Macedonian Empire governed by Perdiccas, Alexander the Great's chief cavalry commander and supreme regent following Alexander's sudden death in 323 BCE. Struggling to preserve imperial unity against rival Diadochi generals, Perdiccas launched an invasion of Ptolemaic Egypt where he was assassinated by his own mutinous officers in 321 BCE.

media.title: First War of the Diadochi - Alexander's Successors At War DOCUMENTARY

name: Kalinga
description: An ancient coastal realm stretching between the Mahanadi and Godavari rivers in modern Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh. Renowned for maritime trade with Southeast Asia, naval prowess, and fierce independence, Kalinga was conquered by Ashoka the Great in a devastating war around 261 BCE that prompted Ashoka's famous conversion to Buddhist non-violence.

media.title: Why The Kalinga War Is The Greatest War In History | Ashoka The Great & Kalinga War

name: Maurya Empire
description: The first pan-Indian empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya and his strategist Chanakya in 322 BCE after overthrowing the Nanda Empire. Reaching its zenith under Ashoka the Great, the Maurya state unified almost the entire subcontinent under centralized bureaucratic rule, disseminating ethical rock edicts, patronizing Buddhism, and standardizing trade.

media.title: Ashoka the Great - Rise of the Mauryan Empire Documentary

name: Polyperchon
description: The Macedonian regency governed by Polyperchon, an experienced veteran commander of Philip II and Alexander the Great appointed supreme regent of the empire in 319 BCE. Opposed by Cassander and rival Diadochi generals, Polyperchon championed Greek liberties and allied with Alexander's mother Olympias during bitter dynastic wars for control of Macedonia.

media.title: Polyperchon, disappears from history in 304 BCE

name: Seleucid Empire
description: The major Hellenistic empire founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 312 BCE following the partition of Alexander the Great's empire, stretching from Anatolia and Syria across Mesopotamia to Bactria. Ruling from Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris, the Seleucid kings established Greek colonist cities and military settlements that cross-pollinated Greek, Babylonian, and Iranian cultures.

media.title: History of the Seleucid Empire | Complete Animated Documentary

name: Atropatene
description: An ancient Iranian kingdom in northwestern Media (modern Iranian Azerbaijan) founded around 323 BCE by the Persian satrap Atropates, who successfully preserved his realm's independence amid the Wars of the Diadochi. Thriving as an autonomous Zoroastrian cultural center, Atropatene gave its name to modern Azerbaijan while skillfully maneuvering between Seleucid, Parthian, and Roman imperial spheres.

media.title: The History Of Atropatene

name: Colchis
description: An ancient Georgian kingdom situated along the eastern Black Sea coast in modern western Georgia, famous in Greek myth as the destination of Jason and the Argonauts for the Golden Fleece. Blessed with rich alluvial gold deposits, timber, and fertile coastal valleys, Colchis was a thriving hub of Black Sea trade and metallurgy.

name: Antigonid Dynasty
description: The Macedonian royal house founded by Antigonus I Monophthalmus ('the One-Eyed'), which ruled the kingdom of Macedon throughout much of the Hellenistic period. Reestablished firmly by Antigonus II Gonatas, the dynasty maintained hegemony over mainland Greece until its final defeat by the Roman Republic at the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE.

media.title: Antigonus the One-Eyed: Alexander's most Ambitious General

name: Anurādhapura
description: The first major kingdom of ancient Sri Lanka, established around the historic capital city of Anuradhapura in 377 BCE by King Pandukabhaya. Flourishing for over a millennium, the kingdom engineered monumental hydraulic irrigation reservoirs (tanks) and celebrated Buddhist stupas, officially embracing Theravada Buddhism under King Devanampiya Tissa.

media.title: The Engineering Marvels Of Sri Lanka's Ancient Kingdom Anuradhapura | The Mark Of Empire

name: Early Cheras
description: An ancient Tamil seafaring dynasty of the Sangam period that ruled the Malabar Coast and western Tamil Nadu (modern Kerala and Kongu Nadu). Operating from port capitals like Muziris, the Cheras conducted lucrative direct spice, beryl, and pepper trade with the Roman Empire and neighboring Mediterranean merchants.

media.title: The Chera Dynasty: Trade, Literature, and the Spice Route

name: Early Cholas
description: An ancient Tamil dynasty of the Sangam period that governed the fertile Kaveri River delta in eastern Tamil Nadu from capitals at Uraiyur and Puhar (Kaveripoompattinam). Celebrated in early Tamil poetry under legendary King Karikala, the early Cholas engineered early flood embankments, established overseas trade with Southeast Asia, and patronized classical Sangam literature.

media.title: The Cholas Naval Power and Temple Building

name: Early Pandyas
description: An ancient Sangam-era Tamil dynasty centered at the cultural capital of Madurai and the pearl-fishing port of Korkai in southern Tamil Nadu. Renowned as the historic patrons of the literary Tamil Sangam assemblies, the Pandyas exported exquisite natural pearls and gemstones across the ancient Mediterranean and Indian Ocean worlds.

media.title: Pandyan Empire – History, Expansion

name: Aetolian League
description: A hardy federal confederation of mountain communities and city-states in central Greece that emerged as a major military power during the Hellenistic era. Governed by a representative council, the league repelled Celtic invaders at Delphi, contested Macedonian dominance, and allied with Rome before disastrously siding with Antiochus III against Roman expansion.

media.title: Aetolian League

name: Kingdom of Pontus
description: A powerful Hellenistic kingdom on the southern Black Sea coast of northern Anatolia, founded by the Persian Mithridatic dynasty. Melding Greek, Persian, and Anatolian cultures, Pontus expanded rapidly under King Mithridates VI Eupator, who waged three fierce wars against Roman hegemony before final defeat by Pompey.

media.title: Kingdom of Pontus

name: Achaean League
description: A federal confederation of Greek city-states based in the northern Peloponnese, which expanded under statesman Aratus of Sicyon to incorporate Corinth, Argos, and Megalopolis. Championing Greek unity against Spartan and Macedonian dominance, the league was the last bastion of Greek political autonomy before its defeat and dissolution by Rome in 146 BCE.

media.title: A Brief Overview of the Achaean League

name: Galatia
description: A highland territory in central Anatolia settled in the 3rd century BCE by migrating Celtic Gauls (Tectosages, Tolistobogii, and Trocmi). Operating as feared mercenary warriors throughout the Hellenistic Wars, the Galatian tribes maintained distinctive Celtic customs, language, and tetrarchic governance until becoming a client kingdom and Roman province.

description: An influential Hellenistic kingdom in western Anatolia ruled by the Attalid dynasty from the dramatic acropolis of Pergamon. Celebrated for patronage of the arts, the great Library of Pergamon, and the monumental Pergamon Altar, the kingdom allied closely with Rome until its last ruler bequeathed the realm to the Roman people in 133 BCE.

media.title: The Rise and Fall of the Attalid Dynasty: From Pergamon’s Glory to Roman Conquest

name: Paphlagonia
description: A rugged ancient region on the Black Sea coast of north-central Anatolia, situated between Bithynia and Pontus. Inhabited by an ancient Anatolian people renowned in antiquity for cavalry and timber, Paphlagonia maintained semi-independent native dynasts before being divided between Pontus, Bithynia, and Roman provincial administration.

name: Antigonid Macedonia
description: The restored Macedonian kingdom under Antigonid rule, serving as the strategic and military northern bulwark of the Hellenistic Greek world. media.title: The Animated History of the Antigonids

name: Greek Colonies
description: The energetic Archaic and Classical diaspora of self-governing Greek settlements established across the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts from the 8th to 6th centuries BCE. From Magna Graecia in southern Italy and Sicily (Syracuse) to Massalia in Gaul and the Black Sea, these colonies spread Greek civic institutions, commerce, and Mediterranean maritime culture.

name: Mamertines
description: A band of Campanian mercenary soldiers originally hired by Agathocles of Syracuse who mutinied, seized the strategic city of Messina in Sicily in 289 BCE, and conducted piracy. name: Âu Lạc
description: An ancient proto-Vietnamese kingdom established in the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam by Thục Phán (King An Dương Vương) around 257 BCE. Centered on the monumental spiral-walled fortress of Cổ Loa, Âu Lạc was celebrated for bronze casting and sophisticated mechanical crossbow technology before being conquered by Nanyue.

media.title: The Story of Au Lac

name: Illyrian Kingdom
description: An ancient Balkan confederation and kingdom of Illyrian tribes situated along the Adriatic coast in modern Albania, Montenegro, and Bosnia. Under rulers like King Agron and Queen Teuta, Illyria fielded formidable lembi warships that dominated Adriatic trade routes, triggering armed conflict and two wars with the Roman Republic.

media.title: History of the Illyrians - Ancient Civilizations DOCUMENTARY

name: Kingdom of Sophene
description: An ancient Hellenistic Armenian kingdom situated in the fertile upper Euphrates valley near modern Elazığ in eastern Anatolia. Positioned along lucrative royal transit routes between Anatolia and Mesopotamia, Sophene was governed by the Orontid dynasty before being incorporated into Greater Armenia by Tigranes the Great.

description: An extraordinary Hellenistic kingdom established around 250 BCE by Diodotus I in Central Asia (modern Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan). Renowned for opulent cities like Ai-Khanoum, magnificent Hellenistic coin minting, and fortified oasis settlements, the kingdom bridged Greek Mediterranean culture with India and the Steppe, eventually expanding south to create the Indo-Greek Kingdom.

media.title: Rise and Fall of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom | The Forgotten Greek Empire in Central Asia

name: Mayan City-States
description: A sophisticated Mesoamerican civilization spanning southeastern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras. Organized into competing city-states like Tikal, Calakmul, and El Mirador, the Maya engineered tropical agriculture, developed the most fully articulated pre-Columbian hieroglyphic script, advanced astronomical mathematics, and monumental corbeled-vault architecture.

description: A Hellenistic kingdom in the highland plateau of central-eastern Anatolia, ruled by an Iranian dynasty that skillfully navigated regional power politics. media.title: The Rise and Fall of Parthia - Rome's Greatest Enemy - Ancient Civilizations

name: Satavahana Dynasty
description: A major Deccan empire that arose in the 2nd century BCE following the decline of the Mauryas, spanning modern Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. Governed from capitals at Pratishthana and Amaravati, the Satavahanas defended central India against Saka incursions, issued multilingual bilingual coinage, and sponsored rock-cut Buddhist chaityas at Karla and Ajanta.

name: Qin Dynasty
description: The short-lived but epochal dynasty (221–206 BCE) that first unified China under Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. Standardizing writing characters, weights, measurements, currency, and axle widths, the regime connected the Great Wall and constructed the Terracotta Army through rigorous Legalist laws, collapsing rapidly in widespread rebellions following the emperor's death.

name: Mauretania
description: An ancient Berber kingdom spanning the Mediterranean Atlantic coast of northwestern Africa (modern northern Morocco and western Algeria). description: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created during the post-Qin Chu-Han Contention in 206 BCE, situated in northern Shanxi and Hebei. description: The dominant hegemony established in 206 BCE by the warlord Xiang Yu after the fall of the Qin dynasty, centered at Pengcheng (modern Xuzhou). description: A formidable pastoral nomadic confederation that unified the Mongolian steppe under Modu Chanyu in the late 3rd century BCE. Fielding hundreds of thousands of horse archers, the Xiongnu built the first great nomadic empire in Inner Asia, extracting trade and tribute from Han China and prompting the construction of the Great Wall.

description: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, covering central Hebei with its capital at Xiangguo. description: The revived principality of Han in the central plains of modern Henan, recreated as one of the Eighteen Kingdoms in 206 BCE. name: Henan
description: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, occupying the strategic heartland of northern Henan centered around Luoyang. Governed by Shen Yang, a former general of Zhao, the small kingdom controlled key Yellow River crossings before submitting to Liu Bang's Han army.

media.title: From Peasant Rebellion to the Rise of Han | Chu-Han Contention

name: Jiaodong
description: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created in 206 BCE on the rugged Shandong Peninsula, with its capital at Jimo. Ruled by Tian Fu, the former king of Qi, Jiaodong was destabilized by internal dynastic rivalries among the Tian clan before being reunified under Qi and eventually subdued by Han.

media.title: Liu Bang vs Xiang Yu: The Human vs the Overlord in Chu-Han Contention

description: A southern principality of the Eighteen Kingdoms established in 206 BCE along the Huai and Yangtze rivers in modern Anhui and Jiangxi. Ruled by the fearsome general Ying Bu, Jiujiang originally served as a vital bulwark for Xiang Yu before Ying Bu defected to Liu Bang, helping secure the Han victory.

description: A northern frontier realm of the Eighteen Kingdoms created in 206 BCE, occupying the Liaodong Peninsula in southern Manchuria. media.title: The ENTIRE history of Han Dynasty: The CHU - HAN Contention

name: Linjiang
description: A southern principality among the Eighteen Kingdoms founded in 206 BCE along the middle Yangtze River in modern Hubei and Hunan. Ruled by Qin rebel leader Gong Ao and his son Gong Wei from Jiangling, Linjiang remained stubbornly loyal to Xiang Yu until captured by Han forces in 202 BCE.

media.title: The Chu–Han Contention: The Civil War That Created the Han Dynasty

name: Nanyue
description: An independent kingdom established in 204 BCE by the Qin general Zhao Tuo, spanning southern China and northern Vietnam (Guangdong, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam) with its capital at Panyu (modern Guangzhou). Blending Han Chinese administrative methods with indigenous Baiyue culture, Nanyue prospered through maritime trade until annexed by Emperor Wu of Han in 111 BCE.

name: Sai
description: One of the 'Three Qins' kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE in eastern Shaanxi, centered at Yueyang. Entrusted to the surrendered Qin general Sima Xin to guard the passes against Liu Bang, Sai was rapidly overrun when Han forces launched their northern offensive.

media.title: From Peasant Rebellion to the Rise of Han | Chu-Han Contention

name: Yin
description: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, situated in northern Henan and southern Hebei with its capital at Zhaoge. Governed by Sima Ang, a former Zhao general, Yin was strategically positioned along the Yellow River before surrendering to Liu Bang's forces in 205 BCE.

name: Yong
description: The primary and largest of the 'Three Qins' kingdoms established in 206 BCE in the central Wei River valley of Shaanxi, centered at Feiqiu. Ruled by Zhang Han, the celebrated former commander-in-chief of the imperial Qin armies, Yong fiercely resisted Liu Bang's invasion before falling after a prolonged siege.

media.title: The Chu–Han Contention: The Civil War That Created the Han Dynasty

name: Han Dynasty
description: The golden age imperial dynasty of China (202 BCE – 220 CE), founded by Liu Bang after the Chu-Han Contention. Establishing Confucianism as the state orthodoxy, the Han created a meritocratic civil service, opened the trans-Eurasian Silk Road, invented papermaking, and expanded imperial borders into Central Asia, Korea, and Vietnam.

media.title: The Han Dynasty Explained

name: Ankhwennefer
description: A native Egyptian rebel pharaoh who, along with his predecessor Horwennefer, led a major nationalist uprising that liberated Upper Egypt from Ptolemaic rule between 205 and 186 BCE. Governing Thebes and surrounding nomes with the support of the Amun priesthood, his rebellion was ultimately crushed by Ptolemy V Epiphanes.

name: Gojoseon
description: The first kingdom of ancient Korea, traditionally established in the Liaoning and northwestern Korean Peninsula around the Taedong River basin. Developing a distinctive Bronze and Iron Age culture characterized by mandolin-shaped daggers and dolmen tombs, Gojoseon challenged Yan and Han China before falling to Emperor Wu of Han in 108 BCE.

media.title: The History of Korea (Ancient Kingdoms to Modern Korea)

name: Kingdom of Numidia
description: A powerful ancient Berber kingdom in northwest Africa (modern Algeria and parts of Tunisia), forged through the unification of the Massylii and Masaesyli tribes under King Masinissa. Famed across antiquity for agile light cavalry that served decisively in the Punic Wars, Numidia clashed famously with the Roman Republic during the Jugurthine War.

name: Korean Jin
description: An ancient proto-Korean confederacy that occupied the southern half of the Korean Peninsula during the 2nd and 3rd centuries BCE. Acting as an agricultural and iron-producing trade nexus between northern Korea and the Japanese archipelago, Jin was the foundational predecessor to the subsequent Samhan confederacies (Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan).

name: Rhodes
description: A major maritime island republic in the southeastern Aegean Sea that flourished as a premier commercial and naval powerhouse during the Hellenistic period. Famed for its maritime code of law, great library, and the colossal bronze Colossus of Rhodes, the island defended freedom of navigation and maintained independence through naval skill and diplomatic neutrality.

name: Mahameghavahana Dynasty
description: A resurgent royal dynasty of ancient Kalinga that restored the region's independence and imperial prestige following the collapse of the Maurya Empire. Its greatest ruler, King Kharavela (2nd century BCE), left the celebrated Hathigumpha rock inscription at Udayagiri, detailing victorious campaigns across North India and generous patronage of Jainism.

media.title: Samrat Kharavela of Kalinga | The Great Jain King of Ancient India

name: Molossians
description: A prominent tribal kingdom of ancient Epirus located in the rugged mountainous highlands of northwestern Greece, centered on the sacred oracle sanctuary of Dodona. Uniting the Epirote tribes under the Aeacid royal house, the Molossians produced celebrated warrior-statesman Pyrrhus of Epirus, famed for his costly victories against the early Roman Republic.

name: Shunga Empire
description: The Magadhan imperial dynasty established in 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga after the assassination of the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha. Ruling from Pataliputra and Vidisha, the Shungas repelled Indo-Greek invasions, patronized traditional Vedic horse sacrifices (Ashvamedha), and sponsored magnificent Buddhist architectural expansions at Bharhut and the Great Stupa of Sanchi.

name: Wusun
description: An ancient semi-nomadic Indo-European pastoral confederation that inhabited the Ili Valley and Issyk-Kul basin of Central Asia (modern Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan). Major players on the northern Silk Road, the Wusun formed strategic diplomatic and marital alliances with Han China to counter their mutual rivals, the Xiongnu steppe empire.

name: Nabataeans
description: An ancient Arab seafaring and caravan trading civilization that dominated the desert crossroads of the southern Levant and northern Arabia. Master hydrologists, they transformed their capital at Petra into a thriving trading hub carved directly into sandstone cliffs, controlling vital incense routes before Roman annexation.

name: Indo-Scythians
description: A confederation of Saka (Scythian) nomadic tribes who migrated from Central Asia into northwestern South Asia (Gandhara, Punjab, Gujarat, and Mathura) during the 1st century BCE. Adopting Buddhism and Indian royal titles while retaining Iranian cavalry traditions, the Sakas established powerful satrapies that influenced North Indian coin design, art, and urban governance.

name: Judea
description: The mountainous biblical heartland in the southern Levant, which endured through Persian, Hellenistic, Hasmonean, and Roman periods. Centered on Jerusalem and the Second Temple, the province was a vibrant focal point of Jewish religious life and identity, marked by repeated uprisings against Seleucid and Roman imperial rule.

media.title: The Maccabees Explained: Revolt, Hanukkah & the Rise of the Hasmoneans

fallback_image.label: Ancient Levant and Arabia in general

name: Indo-Greeks
description: The Hellenistic kingdom established in the 2nd century BCE when Greco-Bactrian rulers like Demetrius and Menander I expanded into northwestern South Asia (modern Afghanistan, Pakistan, and northwestern India). Famous for artistic bilingual coinage in Greek and Kharosthi, the kingdom fostered the rich synthesis of Greco-Buddhist religion, philosophy, and Gandharan sculpture.

media.title: Ancient Greek Kingdom in India

name: Great Yuan
description: An urbanized Hellenistic civilization in the fertile Fergana Valley of Central Asia (modern Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan), recorded in Chinese chronicles as Dayuan ('Great Ionians'). Famed for walled cities and prized, blood-sweating 'Heavenly Horses', Dayuan fought the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE) against Han China, initiating direct Chinese commercial ties to the West.

media.title: The Greco-Chinese War Over the Heavenly Horses

name: Himyarite Kingdom
description: The dominant South Arabian kingdom that ultimately unified modern Yemen under a single centralized crown by conquering Saba, Qataban, and Hadhramaut. Governed from Zafar in the southern highlands, the Himyarites controlled vital Red Sea maritime commerce and notably adopted Judaism as the state religion in the 4th century CE.

media.title: Himyarite Kingdom: The Forgotten Empire of Pre-Islamic Arabia DOCUMENTARY

name: Byeonhan
description: One of the three Samhan confederacies of southern Korea, situated along the Nakdong River valley in the southeastern peninsula. Renowned across East Asia for exceptionally rich iron mines, Byeonhan exported high-quality raw iron ingots and weaponry to northern commanderies and Yayoi Japan, evolving into the Gaya confederacy.

media.title: Samhan (The Three Hans): 진한 Jinhan; 마한 Mahan; 변한 Byeonhan

name: Dongye
description: An ancient tribal state of the Ye people located along the central eastern coast of the Korean Peninsula in modern Gangwon province. Governed by village headmen without a central monarch, Dongye was celebrated for marine agriculture, hunting, fine horse breeding, and distinctive terraced longhouses before being absorbed by Goguryeo.

media.title: Okjeo & Dongye (Ancient Korean States)

name: Italian City-States
description: The mosaic of ancient urban communities and tribal federations—including Samnites, Sabines, Volsci, Latins, and Campanians—that inhabited the Italian peninsula prior to Roman unification. Fiercely protecting local sanctuaries and democratic assemblies, these peoples engaged in repeated mountain conflicts like the Samnite Wars before gradually integrating into the Roman commonwealth.

media.title: Ancient Italy Before Rome Took Over (800–500 BC)

name: Jinhan
description: One of the Samhan confederacies of southeastern Korea, occupying the valley basins east of the Nakdong River. Composed of twelve walled town-statelets skilled in sericulture and ironworking, Jinhan integrated immigrants from northern commanderies and Gojoseon, eventually developing into the ancient kingdom of Silla.

media.title: Korean Three Kingdoms Period explained (History of Korea)

name: Mahan
description: The largest and most powerful of the three Samhan confederacies, comprising over fifty walled town-statelets across southwestern Korea (modern Gyeonggi, Chungcheong, and Jeolla). An advanced rice-farming society organized around sacred ritual precincts (sodo), Mahan was gradually united by one of its constituent member tribes to form the kingdom of Baekje.

media.title: Samhan (The Three Hans): 진한 Jinhan; 마한 Mahan; 변한 Byeonhan

name: Thracian Kingdom
description: The various historical dynastic realms and tribal unions established by the Thracian peoples across the eastern Balkan Peninsula, southern Romania, and the Aegean coast. Celebrated as skilled horsemen, metalworkers, and peltast infantry, the Thracians maintained vibrant oral and spiritual traditions while contested by Macedonian, Celtic, and Roman imperial armies.

media.title: History of the Thracians - Ancient Civilizations DOCUMENTARY

name: Kanva Dynasty
description: A short-lived Brahmin dynasty of Magadha founded in 73 BCE by Vasudeva after overthrowing the last Shunga monarch, Devabhuti. Governing a contracted territory centered on Pataliputra, the four Kanva kings maintained traditional imperial administration for roughly four decades before Magadha fell under the sway of the southern Satavahanas.

media.title: Ancient Indian History | Shunga Dynasty & Kanva Dynasty

name: Caucasian Albania
description: An ancient kingdom in the eastern Caucasus mountains and Kura River valley, corresponding to modern Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan. Composed of diverse Caucasian tribes, Albania fought against Roman and Persian expansion, later developing its own Caucasian Albanian alphabet and adopting Christianity in the 4th century CE.

media.title: The Other Albania: Lost Kingdom of the Caucasus

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Caucasian Iberia
description: An ancient Georgian kingdom centered on the fertile valley of the Kura River in modern eastern Georgia (Kartli), with its capital at Mtskheta. Strategically guarding key mountain passes between the Steppe, Rome, and Persia, Iberia developed a resilient cultural identity, officially embracing Christianity under King Mirian III around 337 CE.

media.title: Pharasmanes of Iberia & Rhadamistus of Armenia

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Kingdom of Adiabene
description: An ancient client kingdom in Upper Mesopotamia centered at Arbela (modern Erbil), situated between the Roman and Parthian imperial frontiers. Notable for its cultural blend of Assyrian, Iranian, and Hellenistic traditions, the royal house famously converted to Judaism in the first century CE, sending relief to Jerusalem during famines.

media.title: Helena, Queen of Adiabene

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Kingdom of Commagene
description: A prosperous Hellenistic buffer kingdom nestled in the Taurus Mountains along the upper Euphrates in modern southeastern Turkey. Ruled by the Orontid dynasty claiming descent from both Persian kings and Alexander the Great, the kingdom is renowned for the monumental mountaintop sanctuary of Mount Nemrut built by King Antiochus I.

media.title: Mount Nemrud I Remastered

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Kingdom of Gordyene
description: An ancient mountain principality located south of Lake Van in the rugged upper Tigris basin of southeastern Anatolia. Inhabited by fiercely independent Carduchians, Gordyene frequently shifted allegiance between the Roman, Armenian, and Parthian empires to preserve its autonomy along strategic mountain corridors.

media.title: The History of the Kurds in the Ancient Period

fallback_image.label: Ancient Anatolia and the Caucasus in general

name: Kingdom of Osroene
description: A prominent kingdom in Upper Mesopotamia centered on the Hellenistic city of Edessa (modern Şanlıurfa, Turkey). Positioned on lucrative caravan trade routes, Osroene maintained semi-independence under an Arab Abgarid dynasty for centuries, becoming one of the earliest regional states to embrace Syriac Christian culture before direct Roman rule.

media.title: The Life and Reign of Abgar VIII: King of Osroene

name: Lazica
description: An ancient Georgian successor kingdom to Colchis located along the southeastern Black Sea coast in modern western Georgia (Egrisi). Controlling strategic Caucasian alpine trade passes, Lazica was a vital battleground and client buffer state contested between the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) and Sasanian Persian empires.

name: Kingdom of Axum
description: A powerful maritime and trading empire centered in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, flourishing along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Positioned along spice and silk routes connecting Rome to India, Axum developed the Ge'ez script, erected colossal monolithic granite stelae, minted its own gold coinage, and adopted Christianity under King Ezana.

media.title: Kingdom of Aksum: Africa’s Forgotten Superpower | Full Documentary

name: Teotihuacan
description: A colossal pre-Columbian metropolis in the Valley of Mexico that was one of the largest cities in the ancient world, peaking around 400 CE. Known for its grid layout, apartment compounds, and monumental Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead, Teotihuacan projected profound cultural influence across Mesoamerica.

media.title: Teotihuacan: Where One Becomes a God

name: Dong-okjeo
description: An ancient tribal state of the Okjeo people located along the narrow coastal strip and mountain valleys of northeastern North Korea and southeastern Manchuria. Dependent on agriculture, fishing, and cloth production, Dong-okjeo lacked a unified king and was repeatedly subjected to tributary subjugation by neighboring Gojoseon, Han commanderies, and expanding Goguryeo.

media.title: Okjeo & Dongye (Ancient Korean States)

name: Goguryeo
description: A powerful ancient kingdom of northern Korea and southern Manchuria, traditionally founded in 37 BCE in the rugged mountain valleys of the Yalu River basin. Renowned for fierce martial culture, heavily armored cataphract cavalry, and impregnable mountain fortresses, Goguryeo expanded into a dominant regional empire, becoming one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea.

media.title: Goguryeo: The Three Kingdoms Period

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman state under Augustus and his successors, which grew from the Roman Republic into a Mediterranean-wide empire.

media.title: Secrets of the Roman Empire

name: Indo-Parthians
description: An ancient kingdom established around 19 CE when the Parthian general Gondophares broke away from the Arsacids to forge an independent realm spanning modern Afghanistan, Pakistan, and northwestern India. Governed from Taxila, the dynasty blended Parthian, Scythian, and Hellenistic cultural traditions, featuring prominently in early Christian apocrypha concerning Saint Thomas.

media.title: The short-lived Iranian dynasty of Ancient India

name: Divergence of the hominin lineage
description: Around seven million years ago, the ancestral lineage leading to humans diverged from the lineage leading to chimpanzees. Fossils recovered from this window, most notably the cranium of Sahelanthropus tchadensis in northern Chad and the femoral remains of Orrorin tugenensis in Kenya, display early anatomical adaptations toward upright bipedal posture, which became the defining locomotion strategy distinguishing hominins from all other hominoids.

media.title: Seven million years of human evolution
media.credit: American Museum of Natural History, YouTube

name: Earliest stone tools (Lomekwian)
description: Archaeologists working at the Lomekwi 3 site discovered the oldest known intentionally flaked stone implements, pushing tool manufacture hundreds of thousands of years earlier than previously assumed. These massive basalt cores and anvils demonstrate deliberate block-on-block percussion used to crack hard plant foods or bone, proving that stone tool knapping predated the emergence of the genus Homo.

media.title: The oldest archaeological site in the world

name: Systematic Oldowan flake tools
description: The Oldowan tradition marked the onset of standardized, systematically produced lithic reduction. Hominins deliberately struck river cobbles with hammerstones to produce sharp-edged flakes and chopper cores, giving our ancestors the butchery tools required to cut tough hides, strip meat from scavenged carcasses, and access lipid-dense bone marrow.

media.title: The Oldowan stone tool

name: Acheulean handaxe technology
description: The Acheulean techno-complex introduced symmetrical, bifacially flaked teardrop handaxes, picks, and cleavers, demanding significant cognitive foresight and mental template mapping compared to earlier flake tools. This versatile toolkit spread across Africa, western Europe, and southern Asia, serving as the dominant hominin tool form for well over one million years.

media.title: Acheulean technology and how to make a handaxe

name: First controlled use of fire
date_text: c. 1 million years ago (evidence at the site may reach 1.79 million)
description: Microscopic analysis of burned bone fragments and plant ashing deep within Wonderwerk Cave confirms that hominins were deliberately managing fire in enclosed shelters by one million years ago. Regular access to fire dramatically lowered digestion costs through cooking, expanded available dietary calories, offered nocturnal defense against apex predators, and lengthened social contact hours after dark.

media.title: When humans first controlled fire

name: Emergence of anatomically modern humans
description: Cranial and dental remains excavated alongside Middle Stone Age tools at Jebel Irhoud pushed the physical origin of our own species back past 300,000 years. These fossils exhibit modern facial morphologies paired with more archaic, elongated braincases, suggesting that modern humans emerged across Africa as a whole rather than in a single local cradle.

media.title: Where the first anatomically modern humans were found

name: Early symbolic and decorative culture
description: Excavations at Blombos Cave recovered smoothed red ochre plaques engraved with cross-hatched geometric patterns, deliberate shell beads pierced for suspension, and dedicated pigment-processing abalone kits. These artifacts constitute some of the earliest conclusive archaeological evidence of modern human symbolic thought, non-verbal communication, and distinct personal ornamentation.

media.title: Blombos Cave: the birth of symbolic thinking

name: Seafaring to Sahul
date_text: 65,000–50,000 years ago (the earliest dates are debated)
description: Modern human populations crossed Wallacea by watercraft to reach the Pleistocene continent of Sahul, joined Australia and New Guinea, with early cultural deposits at the Madjedbebe rockshelter. Because Sahul stayed separated from Asia by deep ocean channels throughout the Pleistocene, reaching it required intentional, multi-stage open-water voyaging and planned maritime exploration.

media.title: The oldest evidence of human seafaring

name: First figurative and narrative cave art
description: Uranium-series dating of calcite crusts overlaying cave wall paintings at Leang Karampuang identified representational art showing human-like figures interacting with a wild pig. This find predates the famous cave art sites of western Europe, showing that narrative painting and visual storytelling were established long before the Last Glacial Maximum.

media.title: Oldest cave art found in Sulawesi

name: Invention of pottery
description: Radiocarbon dates from Xianrendong Cave confirmed that hunter-gatherer bands manufactured fire-hardened ceramic vessels thousands of years before the advent of agriculture. These early pots enabled mobile foragers to boil tough wild seeds, extract bone greases, process freshwater mollusks, and cook stews in durable, flame-tolerant containers.

media.title: The world's first pottery is older than you think

name: Domestication of the dog
description: Genetic and skeletal evidence shows that Eurasian gray wolf populations integrated into human hunter-gatherer camps toward the end of the Pleistocene, becoming our first animal domesticates. Joint burials, such as the Bonn–Oberkassel grave holding two humans and a cared-for puppy, highlight their integration into human foraging, sentry duty, and social structures.

media.title: How dogs (eventually) became our best friends

name: Birth of agriculture (Neolithic Revolution)
date_text: c. 9000 BCE (10,000–8000 BCE across the Fertile Crescent)
description: Hunter-gatherers in Southwest Asia began selecting and cultivating founder crops, including emmer wheat, einkorn, barley and lentils, alongside domesticating sheep and goats. This transition from foraging to food production drove permanent village life, food surpluses, land tenure, and substantial regional population growth.

media.title: Agriculture, part 1
